title: Interview red flags: trade-offs and vector databases
oneliner: Two instant red flags (warning signs) in AI architect interviews: not knowing model trade-offs (when large vs small, high vs low accuracy) and not knowing how to use a vector database.
says: Red flags when interviewing for an AI architect role. First, being unable to explain trade-offs: when to use a large language model versus a small one, when to go for a high-accuracy model versus a cheaper, lower-accuracy one. If you know nothing about trade-offs, that is a red flag. Second, vector databases: an AI architect implementing AI projects must know how to use a vector database properly; not knowing is a red flag.
explained: The trade-off point is the deeper one. Architecture is the discipline of choosing under constraints - cost, latency, accuracy, privacy. A candidate who says 'use the best model' has revealed they have never owned a budget or a latency budget. The LLM/SLM split echoes his inference-economy reel: most tasks are easy and should be cheap; hard tasks justify expensive models. Interviewers probe this because it separates architects from enthusiasts.

The vector database point is about retrieval literacy. Nearly every enterprise AI feature - search, assistants, copilots - retrieves context from a vector store before the model answers. Knowing how embeddings are chunked, indexed, and queried is table stakes (the minimum expected knowledge) for designing those systems, which is why its absence reads as a red flag. His RAG-as-a-service episode in Season 2 is the platform-scale version of this skill.
takeaway: Before any AI architect interview: rehearse your model-selection trade-off logic and be able to design a vector-search flow end to end.
